name: Beth Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wear three hats. On Sundays and Wednesday nights I'm the music director at a big church on the east side of town, leading a band of volunteers from the keyboard. Weekdays I run my own little studio from my flat, writing jingles, which are short advert tunes, and background music for local businesses: a car dealer, two dentists and a radio station's adverts. In the evenings I teach piano, half online and half in person.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I love is building something from nothing: a client says they want people to feel safe at the dentist, and an hour later there's a tune. I use AI tools every single day, for sketching melodies, cleaning up mixes and doing my invoices, and they've doubled what I can get through. What wears me out is chasing small businesses for payment, and the Sunday mornings when the drummer doesn't show. I share a flat with my younger sister Amina, who's studying nursing, and I help her with rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's a fine world for me. The tools I already use stay useful, and nobody floods my market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was a good tool that got oversold, which is what I think already. At church I'd tell the band nothing changes, keep practising. Online I'd post a little clip of how I use it, because clients like seeing the process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is close to ideal. I'm faster than the studios that don't use the tools, and the businesses that hire me still don't want to make their own jingles. My savings cover about four months, the church pay is steady, and I've got more work than hours most months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the studio and take on two or three more businesses, maybe a local furniture chain that's been asking. I'd keep my rate where it is, because being quick and affordable is my edge. And I'd put a bit more into savings, so I'm at six months by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Calm, and a bit pleased with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting paid on time, that's about it. The car dealer paid me ninety days late last year, and that one invoice was half a month's rent. I've started asking for half up front, and most clients don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amina's in her second year of nursing, so she'll have a solid job. I cover about a third of her share of the rent until she qualifies, and our parents do the rest. It's what family does, and she'd do the same for me.

say: AI was a **good tool** that got oversold.
I'd post **a clip** of how I use it, because clients like seeing the process.
think: This is **close to ideal**: I'm faster than studios that skip the tools.
With **four months saved** and steady church pay, I've more work than hours.
do: Take on **two or three** more local businesses, like the furniture chain.
Keep my rate where it is, since **quick and affordable** is my edge.
Grow savings to **six months** by next summer.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit pleased with myself.
S0.quote: The car dealer paid me ninety days late last year, and that one invoice was half a month's rent.
fieldNote: Beth sees AI as **her edge**; the plateau suits her business well.
Her only stated pressure is **late payment**, now handled by asking for deposits.
She supports her sister's rent as a **family duty**, not a burden.

steps.text: Take on two or three more local businesses, like the furniture chain
Ask new jingle clients for half the fee up front
Build savings from four to six months by next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Writing, checking, planning, answering customers. If AI can do all that, it can write a jingle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is the best thing that's happened to small creative businesses, because I'd want clients to keep seeing me as the person who knows the tools. At church I'd keep things calm. Online I'd keep posting how-to clips, because that's free advertising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my studio is right in the path. If a dentist can type 'calm, friendly, fifteen seconds' into an app and get a jingle for nothing, why pay me four hundred dollars? The tools that made me fast make my clients fast too, and the jingle money is about half my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop selling jingles and start selling the whole sound of a business: the jingle, the hold music on the phone, the shop playlist and the video soundtracks, managed every month for a fee. I'd sign the dentists and the car dealer up to monthly retainers, maybe a hundred and fifty dollars each, before they work out they can do it themselves. And I'd push the church elders for a proper part-time contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it's a nervous I know. It's the same feeling as opening the studio three years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You believe in free markets. Is it fair for a dentist to use the free app instead of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely fair, that's the market. Nobody owes me a living, and I'd never ask the government to stop a dentist saving money. My job is to be worth more than the free thing, and if I can't be, I should do something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if half the jingle work goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new keyboard I've been eyeing for a year. Then eating out, which Amina and I do too much anyway. I wouldn't touch what I give her for rent; that's family.

say: AI is **the best thing** for small creative businesses, and I know the tools.
I'd keep posting **how-to clips** online, because that's free advertising.
think: My studio is **right in the path**; a dentist could make a jingle for free.
Jingle money is **about half** my income, and the tools speed up clients too.
do: Sell businesses their **whole sound** monthly: jingle, hold music, playlists and video soundtracks.
Sign clients to **retainers** of about a hundred and fifty dollars a month each.
Ask the church elders for a proper **part-time contract**.
feel: **Nervous**, but familiar, like opening the studio three years ago.
S1.quote: Nobody owes me a living, and I'd never ask the government to stop a dentist saving money.
fieldNote: Beth admits the tools that **made her fast** also make her clients self-sufficient.
She accepts the market as **fair** and refuses to ask government for protection.
She protects her sister's **rent help** first when picturing cuts.

steps.text: Sign the dentists and car dealer to monthly music retainers
Ask the church elders for a proper part-time contract
Put off buying the new keyboard and eat out less

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's the end of the studio, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing I'd say about any big market change: adapt or get left behind. At church I'd tell people to look after each other, because I think a lot of families in our congregation would be hit at once. I'd be honest online that my business is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the studio's gone. Full AGI can do everything I do at the desk, writing, arranging, mixing and client emails, and it'll do it for pennies. What's left is the church, which is people in a room, and in-person piano lessons. That's maybe forty percent of what I earn now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd raise my rates for the clients I have and bank everything, aiming for six months' savings before it lands. I'd move all my teaching to in person, because online lessons are just a screen and the AI will be a better screen. And I'd start building a small business I can actually own: worship music training for smaller churches in the region, Saturday workshops with people in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. But I'd rather be scared and busy than scared and sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sound volunteer Gareth supervises a call centre, and half the people in my Wednesday rehearsal work in offices, in insurance and banking. If they're all losing work in the same year, the collection shrinks and so does my church salary. I'd be worrying about them and about me at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AGI itself to build the new business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, I'd be foolish not to. It'd do my booking, my marketing and my lesson plans, so all my hours go into the room with people. The point is to own something the machine helps with, not something the machine replaces.

say: **Adapt** or get left behind, same as any big market change.
At church I'd tell people to **look after** each other, since families will be hit together.
think: The **studio's gone**: AGI does writing, arranging, mixing and emails for pennies.
Church and in-person lessons leave about **forty percent** of my income.
do: Raise rates and **bank everything**, aiming for six months saved.
Move all teaching **in person**, since AI will be a better screen.
Start **Saturday workshops** training worship musicians at smaller churches.
feel: **Alarmed**, but I'd rather be scared and busy than scared and still.
S2.quote: The point is to own something the machine helps with, not something the machine replaces.
fieldNote: Beth expects to lose about **sixty percent** of her income, mostly desk-based studio work.
She worries her church salary depends on **office workers** in the congregation.
She'd use AGI to **run a business** she owns, rather than resisting it.

steps.text: Raise rates for current jingle clients and bank everything toward six months
Run Saturday worship-music workshops for smaller churches in the region
Hand booking, marketing and lesson plans to AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 32. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. At church I'd offer a free evening for members who want to talk through what they'll do. Online I'd keep it upbeat and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still lose the studio, but I'd have time to wind it down and build the next thing. Five years is enough to get the worship training business going properly and to put money away. I'd be worried, though, because building a new business from scratch is hard, and I've only done it once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd keep the studio running and use it to fund the workshops, starting with three churches near us. I'd take a short course in event management or small-business accounts, because I'd be running bigger things. And I'd invest a bit, maybe two thousand dollars, in a portable keyboard rig and a projector for the workshops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. A bit anxious at night, but focused during the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the workshops don't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go back to the church and ask for full time, and teach piano in person the rest of the week. I'd be poorer but fine. My grandad ran a corner shop for forty years and changed what he sold every few years, and he never once asked for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the robot timing, around 2034, change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me. My work is mostly thinking work and people work, so the robots aren't really my problem. The thinking part lands in 2031, and the people part is what I'm betting on.

S3.quote: My grandad ran a corner shop for forty years and changed what he sold every few years, and he never once asked for help.
fieldNote: Beth uses the five years to **fund the next business** from the dying one.
Her fallback is modest: **full-time church** work and in-person lessons.
Her grandad's **corner shop** is her model for changing with the market.

steps.text: Pilot worship training workshops with three nearby churches
Take a short course in small-business accounts
Spend about two thousand dollars on a portable keyboard rig and projector

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a couple of business cycles. I'd be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for any business owner to get ready, and I'd say it confidently. At church I'd encourage the young ones to learn a trade or a people job alongside their music. Online I'd do a series on how I'm planning for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I think I'm fine. I'd move from jingles to workshops gradually, and by 2036 I'd have a business built on people in a room. What's on my mind is everyone else at church, and whether Amina's hospital ends up with fewer nurses when robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the studio as it is for now and start the workshops slowly, one Saturday a month this year. I'd put a hundred dollars a month into an index fund, so I'm not relying only on myself. And I'd keep learning every new tool as it comes out, because staying early is what's worked for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mild way. It's like a long drive with a storm forecast for the end of the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. What would prove you wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If people stop going to church, or stop paying for anything live because a screen is good enough. Then my bet on people in a room is wrong. I don't think it will happen, but I watch the attendance numbers every Sunday now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister to finish nursing and to get good at the parts a robot can't do, like calming a frightened patient at three in the morning. And I'd tell her to save, even a little, from her first paycheque.

Young church musicians should learn **a trade** or a people job alongside music.

S4.quote: I'd tell my sister to finish nursing and to get good at the parts a robot can't do, like calming a frightened patient at three in the morning.
fieldNote: With a decade, Beth shifts concern from herself to **her community**.
Her bet is on **people in a room**, and she now watches church attendance.
She mixes self-reliance with **modest investing** so she isn't relying only on herself.

steps.text: Keep the jingle studio running as it is for now
Hold one Saturday worship workshop a month this year
Put a hundred dollars a month into an index fund
Try every new AI music tool as it comes out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough time to turn a desk business into a people business. What would help is less red tape for small businesses starting up, and maybe tax breaks for people who reinvest in new ventures. I don't want a cheque, I want room to build.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people at my church would face this through prayer and each other before they'd ever look to the government. A church that sings together on a Sunday is something no app can sell you.

headlineQuote: A church that sings together on a Sunday is something no app can sell you.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old keyboardist** who leads church music, writes jingles and teaches piano.
She uses **AI every day** and sees it as her edge, until clients can use it too.
A **free-market believer**, she says nobody owes her a living and wants no protection.
Her plan across scenarios is a **people-in-a-room** business of worship workshops.
She helps her nursing-student sister **Amina** with rent and treats it as family duty.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: too little time to turn a desk business into a people business.
whatWouldHelp: **Less red tape** and tax breaks for people who reinvest in new ventures.
